summary: Boom bap (90s East Coast hip hop): 85-95 BPM, sampled SP-1200/MPC60 drums with a hard kick and snare on 2 and 4 and MPC-swung hats, a round upright bass on the roots, jazzy 7th chords chopped from a dusty piano or Rhodes, horn phrases; knowledge/style/boombap.json is its template
body: Drums: sampled breaks on an E-mu SP-1200 or Akai MPC60: a hard, punchy kick and a big, snappy snare on 2 and 4, loud and dry; closed hats in 8ths or 16ths swung (MPC swing 58-66%), laid back; kicks on 1 and the off-beats, a second bar that varies. The SP-1200's 26 kHz, 12-bit grit is part of the sound; a slow-attack compressor lets the hits breathe.
Bass: round and simple, an upright or a warm electric bass on the roots (root-seventh-fifth lines), landing with the kick.
Harmony: chopped jazz and soul samples: 7th and 9th chords on piano, Rhodes or horns, two-chord vamps or ii-V, short loops re-triggered each bar rather than held pads; bit-crushed and a little dark.
Lead: there is often none beyond the sample; a horn stab or short muted-trumpet or vibes phrase answers the loop.
Texture/master: dusty and gritty but punchy and loud, the drums on top; softer and low-passed it becomes lofi (production/lofi, genre/lofi-hip-hop).
Sources (2026-11-26): Native Instruments 'What is boom bap' and 'Hip hop drums 101'; MusicRadar 'How to program an old-school hip-hop beat in your DAW' and '12 classic hip-hop production tricks'.
Apply: pattern/boombap-1 on the drums, then pattern/lofi-vamp-vi-iv on the keys four bars later. For a whole style change the Team Lead's restyle uses knowledge/style/boombap.json instead.

drums.about: the drum track (a kit); leave out if there isn't one

keys.about: a chordal part (keys, pad); leave out if there isn't one

key.about: the project's key; leave out to estimate it from the notes
